prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

UNITED NATIONS (CNN) -- More than one million people in Darfur are at risk of losing food, water and shelter in coming months, following the expulsion of international aid groups by Sudan's government, the United Nations' chief humanitarian coordinator said Tuesday. A Doctors without Borders medic helps a sick child in a Darfur refugee camp. The statement by coordinator John Holmes comes after a joint U.N.-Sudanese assessment of the situation. The information was gathered from March 11-18 in hopes of stemming further troubles in Darfur after Sudan's government expelled 13 international relief organizations from the wartorn region. The announcement came on the same day that President Omar al-Bashir, now an indicted war criminal, ignored the threat of arrest by traveling abroad to Eritrea. Also Tuesday, a Sudanese staffer working for a Canadian relief group was shot dead in Darfur. A full report of the assessment will be released soon, according to the U.N., but an executive summary and recommendations were made available on Tuesday. "While a significant effort is being made by the government, by the U.N., by the NGOs [nongovernmental organizations] which are left, to plug some of the immediate gaps in these areas, these are at the same time, 'Band-Aid' solutions, not long term solutions," Holmes said. The U.N. estimates that 1.5 million people in Darfur are dependent on healthcare support, 1.1 million need regular food aid, and another 1 million are in need of clean drinking water. The summary released Tuesday said the World Food Programme, which is still allowed to operate in Sudan, is carrying out a one-time-only distribution program in March and April, but that new partners will be needed to continue delivering food after April. After the International Criminal Court charged Bashir with war crimes and crimes against humanity on March 4, Khartoum expelled 13 international aid agencies and revoked the permits of three organizations in the country. Bashir -- the first sitting head of state to be charged with war crimes by the court -- has continued to say that humanitarian efforts in the country should be "Sudanized." "Within a year, we don't want to see any foreign aid group dealing with a Sudanese citizen," he said at a rally a week after his arrest warrant was issued. Holmes said that 13,000 to 14,000 aid workers in the region already were Sudanese nationals. Holmes said the cooperation and technical help from the Sudanese government on the assessment was a good step forward. But he called it "only the first of many steps if the people in Darfur are not going to suffer major consequences from these expulsions." Sudan's U.N. Ambassador, Abdalmahmood Abdalhaleem Mohamad, has repeatedly said he has information implicating the ousted organizations in activities contrary to their humanitarian missions. He has yet to make any of that information public. One claim is that some organizations acted as spies for the International Criminal Court. Holmes denied those allegations, saying they remain unfounded. "Despite claims that there are dossiers of evidence, we have not been given any of that evidence," he said. "In the absence of that, no meaningful investigation can be done." The British aid organization, Oxfam, one of the agencies expelled from Sudan, released a statement in response to Tuesday's findings. "Current stop-gap measures will only be effective for a short time," the statement said. "As the rainy season arrives within the next two months, people living in weak temporary shelters, in flood-prone locations where latrines can fill and overflow, will become at extreme risk of disease and death. "With the humanitarian capacity reduced by nearly 50 percent, responding to such emergency scenarios will be an enormous challenge for others to tackle," Oxfam said.

The United Nations estimates that 1.5 million people in Darfur depend on healthcare support, 1.1 million require regular food assistance, and another 1 million need clean drinking water.

The summary released Tuesday said the World Food Programme, which is still permitted to operate in Sudan, is conducting a one-time distribution program in March and April. However, new partners will be needed to continue food deliveries after April.

“Within a year, we don’t want to see any foreign aid group dealing with a Sudanese citizen,” he said at a rally one week after his arrest warrant was issued.

Holmes said that between 13,000 and 14,000 aid workers in the region were already Sudanese nationals.

He described the Sudanese government’s cooperation and technical assistance with the assessment as a positive step forward. However, he called it “only the first of many steps if the people in Darfur are not going to suffer major consequences from these expulsions.”

Sudan’s U.N. ambassador, Abdalmahmood Abdalhaleem Mohamad, has repeatedly said he possesses information implicating the expelled organizations in activities inconsistent with their humanitarian missions. He has yet to make any of that information public.

“Despite claims that there are dossiers of evidence, we have not been given any of that evidence,” he said. “In the absence of that, no meaningful investigation can be done.”

Oxfam, a British aid organization and one of the agencies expelled from Sudan, issued a statement in response to Tuesday’s findings.

“Current stop-gap measures will only be effective for a short time,” the statement said. “As the rainy season arrives within the next two months, people living in weak temporary shelters, in flood-prone locations where latrines can fill and overflow, will become at extreme risk of disease and death.

outputs.L2:
**UNITED NATIONS (CNN) —** The Sudanese government’s removal of international relief agencies could leave more than a million people in Darfur without adequate food, clean water or shelter in the months ahead, the United Nations’ top humanitarian official warned Tuesday.

In one Darfur refugee camp, a medical worker from Doctors Without Borders was seen treating an ill child.

U.N. humanitarian coordinator John Holmes issued the warning after Sudanese and U.N. officials jointly evaluated conditions in the region. The assessment was conducted from March 11 through March 18 in an effort to prevent the humanitarian situation from deteriorating further after Khartoum ordered 13 foreign aid organizations to leave the conflict-ravaged area.

The findings were announced as Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir—who has been indicted on war-crimes charges—defied the possibility of arrest by making a foreign trip to Eritrea. Separately on Tuesday, a Sudanese employee of a Canadian aid organization was fatally shot in Darfur.

Although the complete assessment is expected to be published shortly, the United Nations released its executive summary and recommendations Tuesday.

Holmes said Sudan’s government, the United Nations and the nongovernmental organizations that remain in the country are making a substantial effort to address urgent shortfalls. However, he described those measures as temporary “Band-Aid” responses rather than sustainable answers.

According to U.N. estimates, 1.5 million Darfur residents rely on healthcare assistance, 1.1 million require regular food relief and another 1 million need access to safe drinking water.

The summary said the World Food Programme, which retains permission to work in Sudan, was conducting a single round of food distribution during March and April. Other partners, however, would have to be found to keep food deliveries operating beyond April.

On March 4, the International Criminal Court accused Bashir of war crimes and crimes against humanity. In response, the government in Khartoum expelled 13 international relief agencies and canceled the operating permits of three organizations within Sudan.

Bashir is the first serving national leader to face war-crimes charges from the court. He has continued to insist that humanitarian work in Sudan should be transferred to Sudanese control, a policy he has called “Sudanization.”

Speaking at a rally one week after the warrant for his arrest was issued, Bashir said that within a year he did not want any foreign aid organization working directly with Sudanese citizens.

Holmes noted that Sudanese nationals already made up between 13,000 and 14,000 of the region’s humanitarian workers.

He welcomed the Sudanese government’s cooperation and technical assistance during the joint review, calling it a constructive initial move. Nevertheless, Holmes cautioned that it represented only the beginning of a much longer process necessary to prevent Darfur’s population from experiencing severe repercussions because of the expulsions.

Sudan’s ambassador to the United Nations, Abdalmahmood Abdalhaleem Mohamad, has repeatedly asserted that he possesses information showing that the expelled groups engaged in conduct inconsistent with their humanitarian mandates. He has not publicly released any supporting material.

Among the accusations is a claim that certain organizations spied on behalf of the International Criminal Court. Holmes rejected that allegation as unsupported. He said that, despite references to files containing evidence, none of the material had been provided, making a meaningful investigation impossible.

Oxfam, the British relief organization that was among those forced out of Sudan, responded to the findings in a statement Tuesday.

The organization warned that the measures currently filling the gaps would work only briefly. It said the rainy season was expected within two months, placing people in flimsy temporary housing at particularly high risk. Many shelters are in areas vulnerable to flooding, where latrines could fill up and spill over, sharply increasing the danger of illness and death.

Oxfam added that humanitarian capacity had fallen by almost half, meaning other organizations would face an immense challenge if required to respond to such emergencies.

A joint assessment conducted by the United Nations and the Sudanese government found that the measures currently being taken by government agencies, U.N. bodies, and remaining nongovernmental organizations offer only temporary relief. The report described these efforts as “Band-Aid” solutions that cannot meet the population’s longer-term humanitarian needs.

According to U.N. estimates, approximately 1.5 million people in Darfur rely on outside support for healthcare, while 1.1 million require regular food assistance. About one million residents also depend on humanitarian organizations for access to clean drinking water.

The World Food Programme planned a one-time food distribution covering March and April. However, new partner organizations would be needed to maintain food deliveries after that period, raising concerns about potentially severe gaps in assistance.

outputs.L4:
A joint assessment by the United Nations and the Sudanese government has warned of a rapidly worsening humanitarian crisis in Darfur following Khartoum’s expulsion of 13 international aid organizations.

The groups were ordered to leave Sudan after the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for President Omar Hassan al-Bashir over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur. Sudan accused the organizations of cooperating with the court, an allegation the aid agencies denied.

The expelled organizations had provided a substantial share of the food, water, shelter, sanitation and medical services available to civilians displaced by years of conflict. According to the assessment, their departure left major gaps that temporary measures by U.N. agencies, Sudanese organizations and the remaining international groups cannot fill for long.

More than one million people could soon lose access to essential assistance. Food distribution systems face disruption, clean-water facilities require maintenance, medical supplies are running low, and overcrowded displacement camps remain vulnerable to disease outbreaks. The approaching rainy season could further complicate deliveries and increase the risk of waterborne illness.

Although emergency arrangements have prevented an immediate collapse in services, the report cautioned that these stopgap efforts are neither adequate nor sustainable. Remaining organizations lack the staff, equipment, funding and local capacity needed to assume all the work previously carried out by the expelled agencies.

The assessment called for qualified and reliable humanitarian partners to be brought in urgently and given sufficient access to affected communities. Without a durable replacement system, it warned, conditions in Darfur could deteriorate sharply, placing already vulnerable civilians at even greater risk.

Years of fighting among Sudanese government forces, allied militias and rebel groups have displaced millions of people in Darfur. Many continue to depend almost entirely on humanitarian assistance for their basic needs.

### United Nations and CNN: Informing the World

The **United Nations (UN)** is an international organization founded in 1945 to promote peace, security, human rights, and cooperation among countries. Its work includes providing humanitarian aid, supporting sustainable development, addressing climate change, and helping resolve international conflicts.

**CNN**, a global news network, regularly reports on United Nations meetings, peacekeeping missions, humanitarian crises, and diplomatic negotiations. Through live broadcasts, interviews, and analysis, CNN helps audiences understand how decisions made at the UN may affect countries and communities worldwide.

The relationship between international institutions such as the United Nations and media organizations such as CNN highlights the importance of public information. While the UN develops policies and coordinates international action, CNN and other news outlets communicate these developments to a global audience. Independent and responsible reporting enables people to evaluate world events, consider different perspectives, and hold influential institutions accountable.

counterfactuals.output:
**Darfur Faces Deepening Humanitarian Crisis After Sudan Expels Foreign Aid Groups**

**KHARTOUM, Sudan — March 2009** — Millions of people in Sudan’s war-scarred Darfur region face worsening shortages of food, clean water and medical care after President Omar al-Bashir’s government ordered major international aid organizations to leave the country.

Sudanese authorities revoked the registrations of 13 foreign aid agencies and shut down three Sudanese organizations shortly after the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Bashir on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur. The government accused some humanitarian groups of passing information to the court, an allegation rejected by aid organizations and international officials.

The expulsions have removed a substantial part of the humanitarian network supporting Darfur’s vast displaced population. United Nations officials estimated at the time that about 4.7 million people in the region depended on some form of assistance, including roughly 2.7 million people driven from their homes by years of conflict. The expelled organizations were responsible for a significant share of food distribution, health care, sanitation and water services.

Among the agencies affected were organizations involved in running clinics, distributing emergency food, treating malnutrition and maintaining pumps and sanitation systems in camps. Some were also providing protection programs for women and children, agricultural assistance to rural communities and logistical support to other relief operations.

### Camps at immediate risk

The greatest concern centers on Darfur’s crowded displacement camps, where tens of thousands of families live in temporary shelters and rely on humanitarian agencies for basic services. Many camps have limited independent access to water, medicine or food markets.

Aid officials warned that water systems could fail without technicians, fuel and spare parts. A breakdown in sanitation would sharply increase the danger of diarrhea, cholera and other waterborne illnesses, especially as temperatures rise and the rainy season approaches.

Medical services are also under pressure. Clinics operated or supported by expelled organizations treated children suffering from severe malnutrition, pregnant women requiring emergency care and patients with infectious diseases. The departure of foreign staff, combined with the closure or transfer of projects, has left uncertainty over who will provide medicines, trained personnel and referrals for serious cases.

Food supplies may continue temporarily because some stocks and distribution networks remain in place. However, relief officials said the loss of experienced agencies could disrupt registration, transport and monitoring, making it harder to ensure that assistance reaches isolated communities.

### Government says local groups can take over

Sudanese officials defended the decision, saying the expelled organizations had violated national law and that Sudanese agencies and government institutions could assume their responsibilities. Bashir also accused foreign governments of using humanitarian work to interfere in Sudan’s internal affairs.

Khartoum said the expulsions would not lead to a humanitarian disaster and called for the “Sudanization” of aid operations. Authorities argued that national organizations were capable of delivering assistance without the political influence they associated with some foreign groups.

Humanitarian officials, however, said replacing the expelled agencies would require far more than assigning their offices to local organizations. International groups had developed extensive supply systems, technical expertise, donor relationships and trained workforces over several years. Sudanese organizations could play a greater role, they said, but many lacked the money, equipment and access needed to fill the gaps immediately.

The United Nations and donor governments urged Sudan to reverse the expulsions or allow alternative agencies to operate. UN officials stressed that humanitarian assistance should remain separate from the dispute over the ICC warrant.

### Aid workers and civilians caught in political confrontation

The decision followed the ICC’s March 4, 2009, warrant for Bashir, the first issued by the court against a sitting head of state. Prosecutors accused him of directing a campaign of murder, forced displacement, torture and rape in Darfur. Bashir rejected the court’s authority and said the charges were part of a Western conspiracy against Sudan.

The humanitarian organizations affected by the expulsions said they were independent and had not assisted the ICC’s investigation. Several warned that the seizure of property and the sudden removal of staff would make an orderly transfer of programs difficult.

The crisis has also heightened fears for Sudanese employees of international organizations. Thousands of local staff worked as nurses, drivers, engineers, nutrition specialists and community organizers. Some faced the loss of employment, while others were expected to continue operating programs with fewer resources and less international protection.

### Years of conflict and displacement

Darfur’s conflict began in 2003, when rebel groups took up arms against the central government, accusing it of neglecting the western region and discriminating against non-Arab communities. Khartoum responded with a counterinsurgency campaign involving government forces and allied militias widely known as the Janjaweed.

Villages were burned, civilians were killed and large areas were emptied. Sudan’s government has disputed international estimates of the death toll, but humanitarian and research groups have said the violence, disease and hunger associated with the conflict killed hundreds of thousands of people.

Although the intensity of fighting changed over time, insecurity continued to restrict access outside major towns and camps. Aid convoys faced banditry, vehicle theft and attacks, while some rural communities remained beyond the regular reach of relief agencies.

The joint United Nations-African Union peacekeeping mission in Darfur, known as UNAMID, was deployed to protect civilians and support peace efforts. But the force struggled with shortages of personnel and equipment, as well as restrictions on movement.

### Women and children especially vulnerable

Women and children are expected to bear much of the impact of reduced assistance. Women frequently leave camps to collect firewood or seek income, exposing them to harassment and sexual violence. The loss of protection programs and safe spaces could reduce reporting and support for survivors.

Children face heightened risks from malnutrition, interrupted vaccinations and the spread of disease. Education programs may also be affected if agencies can no longer provide teachers, materials or school meals.

Relief officials warned that deterioration may not be immediate or dramatic. Instead, the crisis could deepen gradually as fuel runs out, water pumps break, medicines expire and food-distribution systems lose staff. By the time mortality rates rise, they said, rebuilding the aid network could take months.

For displaced families in Darfur, the expulsions have added another layer of uncertainty to a conflict already marked by repeated displacement and failed peace efforts. Many residents say they fear that a political confrontation between Khartoum and the international community is now threatening the services on which their survival depends.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how the removal of international NGOs from Sudan affected food aid, healthcare, clean water, and emergency preparedness in Darfur, using a CNN-style article.
counterfactuals.output:
# Aid agency expulsions deepen humanitarian crisis in Darfur

**KHARTOUM, Sudan —** Sudan’s removal of major international aid organizations from Darfur disrupted the systems that millions of displaced people relied on for food, medical treatment, clean water and protection from seasonal emergencies.

The government expelled 13 international nongovernmental organizations in March 2009, shortly after the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for President Omar al-Bashir. Sudan accused some groups of cooperating with the court, allegations the organizations denied.

The expelled agencies—including Oxfam, CARE, Save the Children and Médecins Sans Frontières sections—had provided a large share of Darfur’s humanitarian services.

### Food supplies disrupted

The expulsions removed staff and logistical networks responsible for transporting, storing and distributing food. Aid officials estimated that more than 1 million people could face interruptions in food assistance.

Although United Nations agencies and remaining groups tried to fill the gap, they lacked enough workers, vehicles, warehouses and local expertise to quickly replace the expelled organizations. Malnourished children and families living in remote camps were considered especially vulnerable.

### Clinics closed and disease monitoring weakened

Aid groups had operated clinics, vaccination programs, maternal-health services and nutrition centers across Darfur. Their departure reduced access to treatment for an estimated 1.5 million people.

The loss also weakened disease surveillance. Without health workers tracking symptoms and reporting outbreaks, illnesses such as meningitis, measles, malaria and diarrhea could spread before authorities recognized the danger.

### Clean-water systems put at risk

International organizations maintained wells, pumps, latrines and water-treatment systems in crowded displacement camps. When those agencies were expelled, maintenance and sanitation work stopped or was transferred to groups with fewer resources.

Broken pumps or shortages of water-treatment chemicals could quickly leave communities without safe drinking water. Poor sanitation also increased the risk of cholera and other waterborne diseases.

### Emergency preparedness sharply reduced

The timing heightened concern because Darfur’s rainy season was approaching. Heavy rains routinely flood roads, isolate communities, contaminate water sources and increase malaria and diarrheal disease.

The expelled agencies had normally stockpiled food, medicine, fuel and spare parts before roads became impassable. Their removal left less capacity to prepare for floods, disease outbreaks or new waves of displacement caused by fighting.

Sudan said national authorities and remaining aid groups could take over the work. Humanitarian officials warned, however, that replacing years of experience, infrastructure and community relationships could not be done quickly. The expulsions therefore threatened not only daily aid deliveries but Darfur’s ability to withstand the next emergency.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
